newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia waits to see who won poll to end war.
newsitem.headline: Liberia waits to see who won poll to end war.

text.p: Liberians who flocked to vote in elections to end seven years of civil war waited on Sunday to see whether Charles Taylor, the man who started the conflict, would win power through the ballot box.
The count, which began by candlelight, pointed to an unexpectedly close race between Taylor and his main rival, former U.N. Development Programme Africa director Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf.

Spot assessments by reporters of the count after Saturday's election showed the two polling well. Ten other candidates, including Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, two of Taylor's fellow warlords, took part.

Electoral authorities have banned publication of unofficial results, promising to start issuing partial returns from Sunday night or Monday morning. It will not be until Wednesday at the earliest when Liberians' verdict becomes clear.
Taylor, 49, launched the war from Ivory Coast in December 1989.

Both supporters and opponents alike have said his forceful character may offer the kind of leadership needed in the immediate post-war period. He has vastly superior resources to his election rivals and ran a well-oiled electioneering machine.
"God willing, we expect to be elected by a landslide, giving us the mandate that we need coming out of a war situation," a confident Taylor said after casting his vote.
Asked about the possibility of losing, he added:
"We are all winners at this point. I don't think these elections are about losers. These elections are about building this nation to go into the new millennium."

Johnson-Sirleaf entered the political fray late but quickly built up support based on an image of integrity and good contacts with aid donors. Liberian analysts say she could benefit from an anti-Taylor vote if the presidential poll goes to a second round on August 2.
Johnson-Sirleaf, 58, said she believed Liberians had voted wisely. "I feel great. I think the Liberian people are ready for change...ready for a woman (president)."
Despite fears of violence stemming from past faction rivalry, voting passed off peacefully under the scrutiny of more than 500 foreign monitors and regional peacekeeping troops.

Elections commission chairman Henry Andrews said reports from all the country's 13 counties showed a massive turnout and orderly voting. "The mood was good and we have not had any reports about violence or any trouble," he told one reporter.
The West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG, which has policed Liberia since 1990, provided security, stationing soldiers at each polling station. It transported ballot boxes.
"Everything went smoothly. No trouble was reported," force commander General Victor Malu told Reuters.

As a first step towards elections, ECOMOG has disarmed Liberian guerrillas responsible for the war that killed more than 150,000 people. Over half the pre-war population of 2.5 million is displaced and the economy shattered.
Liberia celebrates is 150th birthday on July 26. Freed American slaves founded it as Africa's first modern republic.
Voters were also electing 26 senators and 64 lower house deputies in the poll, based on proportional representation.
